sections.title: Setting up the Difference Quotient
sections.content_markdown: To find the derivative of $f(x) = 1/x$ at a general point $x_0$, we begin by constructing the difference quotient, which represents the slope of the secant line. The formula for the difference quotient is $\frac{\Delta f}{\Delta x} = \frac{f(x_0 + \Delta x) - f(x_0)}{\Delta x}$. Substituting the function $f(x) = 1/x$, we obtain the expression $\frac{\frac{1}{x_0 + \Delta x} - \frac{1}{x_0}}{\Delta x}$. This expression is inherently complex because it involves a difference in the numerator and a difference in the denominator (the change in $x$). At this stage, directly evaluating the limit as $\Delta x \to 0$ results in an indeterminate $0/0$ form, necessitating algebraic simplification before we can proceed to the limit.

sections.title: Algebraic Simplification
sections.content_markdown: To simplify the difference quotient, we first factor out $1/\Delta x$. We then combine the terms in the numerator over a common denominator, which is $(x_0 + \Delta x)x_0$. This yields the expression $\frac{1}{\Delta x} \left( \frac{x_0 - (x_0 + \Delta x)}{(x_0 + \Delta x)x_0} \right)$. Simplifying the numerator, $x_0 - (x_0 + \Delta x)$ becomes $-\Delta x$. The expression now reads $\frac{1}{\Delta x} \left( \frac{-\Delta x}{(x_0 + \Delta x)x_0} \right)$. We can now perform two crucial cancellations: the $\Delta x$ in the denominator and the $\Delta x$ in the numerator cancel out. This leaves us with the simplified expression $-\frac{1}{(x_0 + \Delta x)x_0}$. This form is now amenable to taking the limit, as the problematic division by zero has been removed.

sections.title: Taking the Limit and Plausibility Check
sections.content_markdown: With the expression simplified to $-\frac{1}{(x_0 + \Delta x)x_0}$, we can now take the limit as $\Delta x \to 0$. By setting $\Delta x = 0$, we obtain the derivative $f'(x_0) = -\frac{1}{x_0^2}$. To verify this result, we perform a plausibility check. First, the derivative is negative, which is consistent with the graph of $1/x$ having a negative slope. Second, as $x_0$ increases toward infinity, the magnitude of the slope $-1/x_0^2$ decreases, which matches the visual observation that the curve becomes less steep as we move further to the right. We can further confirm this by substituting a specific value, such as $x_0 = 3$, into the simplified expression, which yields $-1/9$ as $\Delta x$ approaches zero, confirming the general formula.
